'''Elmhurst''' (formerly '''Newtown''') is a [[neighborhood]] in the [[borough (New York City)|borough]] of [[Queens]] in [[New York City]]. It is bounded by [[Roosevelt Avenue]] on the north; the [[Long Island Expressway]] on the south; [[Junction Boulevard]] on the east; and the [[New York Connecting Railroad]] on the west.<ref name="nytimes-elmhurst">{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1985/08/04/realestate/if-you-re-thinking-of-living-in-elmhurst.html |title=If You're Thinking of Living in: Elmhurst |work=[[The New York Times]] |first=Amanda |last=Marques |date=August 4, 1985 |access-date=August 7, 2014}}</ref>

The village, originally named '''Middleburgh''', was established in 1652 by English Puritans, approximately {{Convert|7|mi}} from [[New Amsterdam]]. When the British took over New Netherland in 1664, they renamed it New Town, which was eventually simplified to Newtown. It remained a rural community until the late 1890s, when it was renamed Elmhurst and became part of the [[City of Greater New York]]. Elmhurst became heavily developed with residential and commercial structures in the early 20th century, and many immigrants started moving in during the latter part of the century. The neighborhood is known for its diverse international food scene, featuring Thai, Chinese, Tibetan, Vietnamese, Indonesian, Colombian, Argentine and more.

Elmhurst is located in [[Queens Community Board 4|Queens Community District 4]] and its ZIP Code is 11373.<ref name="NYCPlanning"/> It is patrolled by the [[New York City Police Department]]'s 110th Precinct.<ref name="NYPD 110th Precinct"/> Politically, Elmhurst is represented by the [[New York City Council]]'s 25th District and small parts of the 21st, 24th, and 29th Districts.<ref>[http://www.nyc.gov/html/dc/downloads/pdf/queens.pdf Current City Council Districts for Queens County], [[New York City]]. Accessed May 5, 2017.</ref>

==History==

=== 17th and 18th centuries ===
The village was founded in 1652 in the Dutch colony of [[New Netherland]] ({{lang|nl|Nieuw Nederland}}) by English [[Puritans]] from [[Connecticut Colony|Connecticut]] and [[Massachusetts Bay Colony|Massachusetts]]. They named it {{lang|nl|Middelburgh}} ('Middleburgh') after the capital of the Dutch province of [[Zeeland]], which had been a refuge of Puritans fleeing religious persecution in England. The village was located approximately {{Convert|7|mi}} from the growing city of [[New Amsterdam]] ({{lang|nl|Nieuw Amsterdam}}) and just east of the settlement at Maspat (now called [[Maspeth, Queens|Maspeth]]), which had been abandoned following threats and attacks by local [[Lenape]] Native Americans.<ref name="nytimes-elmhurst" /><ref name="SeyfriedAsadorian2012">{{cite book|author1=Vincent F. Seyfried|author2=William Asadorian|title=Old Queens, N.Y., in Early Photographs: 261 Prints|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qUHCAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA23|date=August 28, 2012|publisher=Courier Corporation|isbn=978-0-486-13601-1|pages=23–}}</ref> When the British took over New Netherland in 1664, they renamed Middleburgh as {{lang|nl|Nieuwe Stad}} (New Town) to maintain a connection to its Dutch heritage.<ref name="SeyfriedAsadorian2012" /> This was eventually simplified to Newtown. In a deed dated July 9, 1666, the settlers took title to the lands of Newtown from the Native American tribes.<ref name="bde18991022">{{cite news|date=October 22, 1899|title=Residences Which Are Historical|page=26|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/clip/4095046/|access-date=July 4, 2020|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com {{open access}}}}</ref>

A town building, near what is now Broadway and Corona Avenue, was erected to serve as both a community and religious building. Use of this building was shared by the different religious denominations in Middleburgh: the [[Church of England]], the [[Dutch Reformed Church]], the [[Presbyterianism|Presbyterians]], and the [[Quakers]].<ref>{{cite web|date=November 12, 1999|title=St. James Church|url=https://catalog.archives.gov/medialz/electronic-records/rg-079/NPS_NY/14000938.pdf|publisher=[[National Register of Historic Places]], [[National Park Service]]|pages=6–7}}{{Dead link|date=January 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> In 1669, the town planned a new church for all of these denominations, on a plot of land donated by Ralph Hunt near Grand Avenue and Queens Boulevard. According to the town records, the new building was to cost forty [[New York pound|pounds]], half in corn and half in cattle.<ref name="btu19270925">{{cite news|date=September 25, 1927|title=Newtown Presbyterians Plan 275th Anniversary Program|page=18|work=Brooklyn Times-Union|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/54638715/|access-date=July 3, 2020|via=newspapers.com {{open access}}}}</ref> The village of Newtown was established as the town seat for the township in 1683,<ref name="nytimes-elmhurst" /> when Queens County was reorganized as a "one county, five towns" model. The Town of Newtown, which had a town hall, jail, tax office, and town clerk's office, was the center of a municipality that comprised the villages that were located north of present-day [[Forest Park (Queens)|Forest Park]] and west of [[Flushing Meadows–Corona Park|Flushing Meadows]].<ref name="SeyfriedAsadorian2012" />

By 1700, the town had a population of 1,000, including 405 youths under the age of sixteen, 434 adults, and 161 slaves.<ref name="bde18991022" /> Among the English settlers in the present Elmhurst section of Newtown was Gershom Moore, who lived at what is now the intersection of Broadway, 45th Avenue, and Elmhurst Avenue. A [[chance seedling]] on his farm eventually produced the [[Newtown Pippin]], Colonial America's most famous apple.<ref>[[David Karp (pomologist)|David, Karp]]. [https://www.nytimes.com/2003/11/05/dining/it-s-crunch-time-for-the-venerable-pippin.html?pagewanted=all "It's Crunch Time for the Venerable Pippin"], ''[[The New York Times]]'', November 5, 2003. Accessed September 20, 2018. "The Newtown Pippin arose in the late 17th or early 18th century as a seedling in the Moore family orchard, which stretched from the East River to what is now 54th Street in Elmhurst (formerly Newtown), Queens."</ref> The [[St. James Church (Queens)|St. James Church]] was founded in 1704,<ref>{{Cite web|last=Ilel|first=Neille|date=August 5, 2004|title=Elmhurst Parish Turns 300; Celebrates With Major Facelift|url=https://www.qchron.com/news/western/elmhurst-parish-turns-300-celebrates-with-major-facelift/article_e614a504-631b-5e2b-8414-ea1421451945.html|access-date=2020-06-21|website=Queens Chronicle|language=en}}</ref> followed by the [[Reformed Church of Newtown]] in 1731.<ref name="renaissance">{{Cite news|last=Kleiman|first=Dena|date=1982-11-15|title=Immigrants Spur Renaissance for Queens Churches|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1982/11/15/nyregion/immigrants-spur-renaissance-for-queens-churches.html|access-date=2020-06-21|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> The Colonel Bernardus Bloom Farmhouse at 90-11 56th Avenue, which existed from the 17th century to 2015, was one of the oldest surviving farmhouses in Newtown through the 21st century.<ref>{{cite web|last=Honan|first=Katie|date=2015-10-23|title=Newtown Civic Association Fights to Save Historic Farmhouse From Demolition|url=https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20151023/elmhurst/newtown-civic-association-fights-save-historic-farmhouse-from-demolition|access-date=2020-06-30|website=DNAinfo New York|archive-date=July 2, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200702004428/https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20151023/elmhurst/newtown-civic-association-fights-save-historic-farmhouse-from-demolition/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

=== 19th century ===
[[File:Old Tracks and Routes in Newtown (Plate LIV, p. 272).jpg|thumb|left|1910 map of old roads in New Town]]
Newtown was also the center of a population of [[African Americans|free blacks]] and slaves by the early 19th century. With the program of gradual abolition and the [[manumission]] of some slaves by masters following the American Revolution, the free population increased.<ref>Peace, Katy. [https://www.preservenys.org/blog/seven-to-save-spotlight-elmhurst-african-american-burial-ground 'Seven to Save Spotlight: Elmhurst African American Burial Ground"], Preservation League of New York State, October 1, 2020. Accessed January 1, 2024. "Newtown, what is now Elmhurst, was settled by free African Americans in 1828, one of several such communities that popped up in New York City after slavery was abolished in 1827 (Seneca Village, which was displaced to create Central Park, might be the most famous of these communities)."</ref> In 1828, a year after [[History of slavery in New York (state)|slavery in New York state was finally abolished]] under the terms of a 1799 gradual abolition law,<ref>Benton, Ned. [https://nyslavery.commons.gc.cuny.edu/dating-the-start-and-end-of-slavery-in-new-york/ "Dating the Start and End of Slavery in New York"], [[John Jay College of Criminal Justice]]. Accessed January 1, 2024. "Slavery officially ended in New York 1827. When the Gradual Emancipation law was passed in 1799 it did not apply to persons enslaved at the time, but gradually emancipated children of enslaved mothers born after the enactment of the law."</ref> landowner James Hunter and his wife deeded {{Convert|2|acres}} to the community for a church and parsonage. They had already been using land at Corona Avenue and 90th Street as a burial ground since about 1818. This was associated with the United African Society of Newtown, by 1906 known as [[St. Mark's A.M.E. Church]]. By 1886, more than 300 burials had been made in the cemetery. The church moved further east and gradually the burial ground was forgotten until the remains of a woman were discovered in an iron coffin in 2011 during development. The church is hoping to buy the land for preservation.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Laterman|first=Kaya|date=2019-06-14|title=This Empty Lot Is Worth Millions. It's Also an African-American Burial Ground.|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/06/14/nyregion/african-american-burial-ground-queens-newtown.html|access-date=2020-07-05|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

More concentrated residential development in the area was spurred by the completion of a horsecar line, the [[Grand Street Line (Brooklyn)|Grand Street Line]], which reached New Town in 1854. The [[Long Island Rail Road]]'s [[Main Line (Long Island Rail Road)|Main Line]] was built through Newtown in 1876, attracting more residents to the neighborhood.<ref name="SeyfriedAsadorian2012"/>

=== Renaming and incorporation into city ===
[[Cord Meyer (New York politician)|Cord Meyer]] bought land at Broadway and Whitney Avenue in 1896. He proposed that the town be renamed "Elmhurst", meaning "a grove of elms"; in 1897, one year before Queens County was incorporated in the [[New York City|Greater City of New York]], the town was renamed.<ref name="SeyfriedAsadorian2012"/> The renaming was done partially to disassociate the town from nearby Maspeth and the smelly, polluted [[Newtown Creek]], and partially to celebrate the [[elm tree]]s (''[[Ulmus americana]]'') that abounded in the area.<ref name=nytimes-elmhurst/><ref name="libra triangle"/>

Elmhurst developed as a fashionable district due to a [[housing development]] built by the Cord Meyer Development Company between 1896 and 1910, north of the [[Port Washington Branch]] railroad [[Elmhurst station (LIRR)|station]]. Cord Meyer expanded its holdings between 1905 and 1930, including Elmhurst Square, Elmhurst South, Elmhurst Heights, and New Elmhurst. Elmhurst also was the site of the [[Grand Street (LIRR Main Line station)|Grand Street LIRR station]] just west of the current [[Grand Avenue – Newtown (IND Queens Boulevard Line)|Grand Avenue – Newtown]] subway station. The Grand Street LIRR station was served by the Main Line and the former [[Rockaway Beach Branch]].<ref name=nytimes-elmhurst/><ref name="libra triangle"/> In the 1930s, the [[Independent Subway System]]'s [[IND Queens Boulevard Line|Queens Boulevard line]] was built through the neighborhood, spurring economic development but also destroying many old buildings.<ref name="SeyfriedAsadorian2012"/>

Prior to World War II, Elmhurst had become an almost exclusively [[American Jews|Jewish]] and [[Italian American|Italian]] neighborhood, made up of early 20th century immigrants and their descendants. Following the war, Elmhurst evolved into what has been considered one of the most [[ethnic diversity|ethnically diverse]] neighborhoods in New York City, as immigrants arrived from new areas.<ref>[https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/middleburgh-triangle/history Middleburgh Triangle], [[New York City Department of Parks and Recreation]]. Accessed January 1, 2024. "Elmhurst, which before World War II had comprised predominantly white, middle-class residential areas with a strong Jewish and Italian influence, has evolved into one of the most ethnically diverse sections of Queens."</ref><ref>{{Cite news|date=1982-10-06|title=A Hospital Where Ethnic Change Is Constant|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1982/10/06/nyregion/a-hospital-where-ethnic-change-is-constant.html|access-date=2020-07-05|issn=0362-4331|quote=Dr. Stanley Bleich had been an intern less than a month at the municipal hospital in Elmhurst, Queens,... one of the city's 16 municipal hospitals, [which] is in what immigration officials have described as the city's most ethnically diverse neighborhood.}}</ref> By the 1980s, there were persons from 112 nations in residence in the neighborhood, which has continued to diversify since then.<ref name=nytimes-elmhurst/> Among the most numerous ethnic groups that have settled in the area are [[Latino (U.S. Census)|Latinos]] and [[Chinese American]]s.<ref name="cny 201502">{{cite web | url=http://www.crainsnewyork.com/article/20150209/REAL_ESTATE/302089995/housing-gains-in-elmhurst-queens-leave-many-cold | title=Housing gains in Elmhurst, Queens, leave many cold | publisher=[[Crain's New York]] | date=February 9, 2015 | access-date=June 8, 2015 | author=Kerry Murtha}}</ref>

For many years, the Elmhurst gas tanks, a pair of large [[natural gas]] [[Gasometer|storage structures]] built in 1910 and 1921 on 57th Avenue between 74th and 80th Streets, were well-known landmarks, standing {{convert|200|feet}} high. Because the [[Long Island Expressway]] frequently became congested in that area, "backup at the Elmhurst Gas Tanks" became a familiar phrase in radio [[traffic reporting]]. The gas storage facilities were removed in 2001.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Hevesi|first=Dennis|date=1993-09-20|title=Memory-Filled Tanks; Queens Loses 2 Roadside Landmarks|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1993/09/20/nyregion/memory-filled-tanks-queens-loses-2-roadside-landmarks.html|access-date=2020-07-05|issn=0362-4331|quote=The Elmhurst tanks — those 200-foot monoliths that stood sentinel to the changing landscape of Queens and as harbingers of hair-tearing delay on the highway to Manhattan — are down, deflated forever, their skeletal remains waiting to be dismantled}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.queenstribune.com/guides/2006_Queens100/OurPast/index.htm |title=Elmhurst gas tanks |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070608101457/http://queenstribune.com/guides/2006_Queens100/OurPast/index.htm |archive-date=June 8, 2007 |work=[[Queens Tribune]] |access-date=June 4, 2007 |quote=But when the beloved landmarks weren't really doing the business anymore they came down in 1996 and by 2001 there was almost no trace of the tanks that once supplied business and homes across the city.}}</ref> The site was redeveloped and opened as [[Elmhurst Park]] in 2011.<ref>[https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/elmhurst-park Elmhurst Park], [[New York City Department of Parks & Recreation]]. Accessed July 7, 2016. "Elmhurst Park, once an eyesore and traffic landmark, opened to the public in 2011 as a magnificent community greenspace. The site of Elmhurst Park was once the location of two KeySpan Newtown gas holders, a highway landmark popularly known as the 'Elmhurst gas tanks.'"</ref>

== Land use ==
Elmhurst contains a variety of [[zoning]] districts, including manufacturing, commercial, residential, and mixed-use. Much of the neighborhood is composed of detached or multi-family houses, though there are also [[rowhouse]] districts, apartment buildings of up to six or seven stories, and large developments such as [[LeFrak City]]. Commercial overlays are located primarily along Queens Boulevard, Broadway, and Grand and Corona Avenues. Several tracts are also zoned for shopping centers, which are occupied by [[#Malls|Elmhurst's malls]]. Light-manufacturing zones are located near the western end of the neighborhood, mainly between the LIRR's Port Washington Branch and 51st Avenue.<ref name="zola-planning-map">{{cite web|title=NYC's Zoning & Land Use Map|url=https://zola.planning.nyc.gov/|access-date=November 17, 2018|publisher=[[Government of New York City|nyc.gov]]}}</ref>

=== Official landmarks ===
Some buildings in Elmhurst are listed on the [[National Register of Historic Places]] (NRHP) and/or are [[New York City designated landmark|designated New York City Landmarks]] (NYCL):

* [[Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks, Lodge Number 878]] (NRHP, NYCL), built in 1923–1924, once the largest [[Elks lodge]] in the [[Eastern United States]]<ref>{{cite web|date=2001-08-14|title=Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks, Lodge Number 878|url=http://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/2086.pdf|access-date=June 11, 2020|publisher=[[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|date=2014-11-19|title=Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks, Lodge Number 878|url=https://www.nps.gov/nr/feature/places/pdfs/14000938.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170202202721/https://www.nps.gov/nr/feature/places/pdfs/14000938.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-date=February 2, 2017|access-date=June 11, 2020|publisher=[[National Register of Historic Places]], [[National Park Service]]}}</ref>
* [[First Presbyterian Church of Newtown]] (NRHP), built in 1895<ref name="NRHP-13000696">{{cite web|date=September 9, 2013|title=First Presbyterian Church of Newtown|url=https://www.nps.gov/nr/feature/places/pdfs/13000696.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170216020056/https://www.nps.gov/nr/feature/places/pdfs/13000696.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-date=February 16, 2017|access-date=June 11, 2020|publisher=[[National Register of Historic Places]], [[National Park Service]]}}</ref>
* [[Newtown High School (Queens)|Newtown High School]] (NYCL), a [[Renaissance Revival architecture|Flemish Renaissance Revival-style]] building erected in 1921 and expanded in 1931<ref>{{cite web|date=2003-06-24|title=Newtown High School|url=http://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/2131.pdf|access-date=June 11, 2020|publisher=[[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]]}}</ref>
* [[Reformed Church of Newtown]] (NRHP, NYCL), one of the oldest wood churches in New York City, first established by [[Dutch people|Dutch]] [[immigrant]]s in 1731<ref>{{cite web|date=1966-07-19|title=Reformed Dutch Church of Newtown and Fellowship Hall|url=http://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/0138.pdf|access-date=June 11, 2020|publisher=[[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|date=April 23, 1980|title=Reformed Church of Newtown Complex|url=https://catalog.archives.gov/medialz/electronic-records/rg-079/NPS_NY/80002751.pdf|access-date=June 11, 2020|publisher=[[National Register of Historic Places]], [[National Park Service]]}}</ref>
* [[St. James Church (Queens)|St. James Church]] (NRHP, NYCL), built in 1735 and the oldest surviving [[Anglican]] building in the city<ref>{{cite web|date=November 12, 1999|title=St. James Church|url=https://catalog.archives.gov/medialz/electronic-records/rg-079/NPS_NY/99001331.pdf|access-date=June 11, 2020|publisher=[[National Register of Historic Places]], [[National Park Service]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|date=2017-09-19|title=Old Saint James Episcopal Church (Old Saint James Parish Hall)|url=http://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/2593.pdf|access-date=June 11, 2020|publisher=[[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]]}}</ref>

The [[Jamaica Savings Bank (Elmhurst, Queens)|Elmhurst branch]] of the [[Jamaica Savings Bank]] was previously a New York City Landmark, but the designation was removed in 2005.<ref>{{cite web|last=Steele|first=Lockhart|date=2005-10-28|title=Elmhurst's Jamaica Savings Bank: Landmark Or Not?|url=https://ny.curbed.com/2005/10/28/10611542/elmhursts-jamaica-savings-bank-landmark-or-not|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200613151106/https://ny.curbed.com/2005/10/28/10611542/elmhursts-jamaica-savings-bank-landmark-or-not|url-status=dead|archive-date=June 13, 2020|access-date=2020-06-13|website=Curbed NY}}</ref>

==Demographics==
Based on data from the 2022 census, the population of Elmhurst was 160,534, an increase of 72,107 from the 88,427 counted in 2010. Covering an area of {{convert|750.28|acres}}, the neighborhood had a population density of {{convert|117.9|PD/acre|PD/sqmi PD/sqkm}}.<ref name="PLP3A">https://furmancenter.org/neighborhoods/view/elmhurst-corona#demographics
Accessed February 2025</ref>

The racial makeup of the neighborhood was 6.7% [[White (U.S. Census)|White]], 8.1% [[African American (U.S. Census)|African American]], 0.2% (133) [[Native American (U.S. Census)|Native American]], 33.8% [[Asian (U.S. Census)|Asian]], 0.0% (28) [[Pacific Islander (U.S. Census)|Pacific Islander]], 0.4% (338) from [[Race (United States Census)|other races]], and 1.6% (1,423) from two or more races. [[Hispanic (U.S. Census)|Hispanic]] or [[Latino (U.S. Census)|Latino]] of any race were 49.6% of the population.<ref name="PLP3A">https://furmancenter.org/neighborhoods/view/elmhurst-corona#demographics
Accessed February 2025</ref> Elmhurst's Latino population is 20.4% South American (9.8% Ecuadorean, 7.2% Colombian, 1.8% Peruvian, 0.4% Argentinean, 0.4% Bolivian, 0.2% Chilean, 0.2% Venezuelan), 11.6% Mexican, 3.1% Dominican, 1.8% Puerto Rican, 1.5% Central American (0.5% Salvadoran, 0.4% Guatemalan, 0.3% Honduran), and 0.7% Cuban.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.census.gov|title=U.S. Census website|publisher=United States Census Bureau|website=[[United States Census Bureau]]|language=en|access-date=2018-03-04}}</ref>

==Police and crime==
Elmhurst and Corona are patrolled by the 110th Precinct of the [[New York City Police Department|NYPD]], located at 94-41 43rd Avenue.<ref name="NYPD 110th Precinct">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/site/nypd/bureaus/patrol/precincts/110th-precinct.page|title=NYPD – 110th Precinct|website=www.nyc.gov|publisher=[[New York City Police Department]]|access-date=October 3, 2016}}</ref> The 110th Precinct ranked 15th safest out of 69 patrol areas for per-capita crime in 2010.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/crime-safety-report/queens/corona/|title=Corona and Elmhurst – DNAinfo.com Crime and Safety Report|website=www.dnainfo.com|access-date=October 6, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170415063655/https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/crime-safety-report/queens/corona|archive-date=April 15, 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref> {{As of|2018}}, with a non-fatal assault rate of 34 per 100,000 people, Corona and Elmhurst's rate of [[violent crime]]s per capita is less than that of the city as a whole. The incarceration rate of 227 per 100,000 people is lower than that of the city as a whole.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|8}}

The 110th Precinct has a lower crime rate than in the 1990s, with crimes across all categories having decreased by 83.2% between 1990 and 2020. The precinct reported 4 murders, 29 rapes, 270 robberies, 359 felony assaults, 196 burglaries, 485 grand larcenies, and 138 grand larcenies auto in 2020.<ref>{{cite web|last=|first=|date=|title=110th Precinct CompStat Report|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/crime_statistics/cs-en-us-110pct.pdf|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180413193406/http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/crime_statistics/cs-en-us-110pct.pdf|archive-date=April 13, 2018|access-date=January 18, 2021|website=www.nyc.gov|publisher=[[New York City Police Department]]}}</ref>

==Health==
{{As of|2018}}, [[preterm birth]]s are less common in Elmhurst and Corona than in other places citywide, but births to teenage mothers are more common. In Elmhurst and Corona, there were 83 preterm births per 1,000 live births (compared to 87 per 1,000 citywide), and 25.8 births to teenage mothers per 1,000 live births (compared to 19.3 per 1,000 citywide).<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|11}} Elmhurst and Corona have a high population of residents who are [[Health insurance coverage in the United States|uninsured]]. In 2018, this population of uninsured residents was estimated to be 25%, which is higher than the citywide rate of 12%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|14}}

The concentration of [[particulates|fine particulate matter]], the deadliest type of [[air pollution|air pollutant]], in Elmhurst and Corona is {{convert|0.0077|mg/m3|oz/ft3}}, slightly higher than the city average.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|9}} Fifteen percent of Elmhurst and Corona residents are [[Smoking|smokers]], which is equal to the city average of 14% of residents being smokers.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|13}} In Elmhurst and Corona, 20% of residents are [[Obesity|obese]], 9% are [[Diabetes mellitus|diabetic]], and 23% have [[hypertension|high blood pressure]]—compared to the citywide averages of 20%, 14%, and 24% respectively.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|16}} In addition, 24% of children are obese, compared to the citywide average of 20%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|12}}

Eighty-eight percent of residents eat some fruits and vegetables every day, which is about the same as the city's average of 87%. In 2018, 68% of residents described their health as "good", "very good", or "excellent", lower than the city's average of 78%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|13}} For every supermarket in Elmhurst and Corona, there are 16 [[convenience store|bodegas]].<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|10}}

The [[Elmhurst Hospital Center]] is located in Elmhurst.<ref>{{cite web | last=Finkel | first=Beth | title=Guide To Queens Hospitals | website=Queens Tribune | date=February 27, 2014 | url=http://queenstribune.com/guide-to-queens-hospitals/ | access-date=March 7, 2019 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170204185507/http://queenstribune.com/guide-to-queens-hospitals/ | archive-date=February 4, 2017 | url-status=dead }}</ref>

Horace Harding Expressway was once a turnpike called Nassau Boulevard, which went from Elmhurst to [[Flushing, Queens|Flushing]], [[Bayside, Queens|Bayside]], and [[Little Neck, Queens|Little Neck]]. It was renamed for [[Horace J. Harding]] (1863–1929), a finance magnate who directed the [[New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad]] and the [[Rapid transit operations of the BRT and BMT|New York Municipal Railways System]]; Harding encouraged city planner [[Robert Moses]]'s system of [[parkway (New York)|parkway]]s on New York, and after Harding died, the boulevard—now the [[service road]] of the [[Long Island Expressway]]—was renamed after him.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://forgotten-ny.com/2013/11/nyc-streets-featuring-full-names/ | title=NYC STREETS FEATURING FULL NAMES | publisher=Forgotten NY | date=November 2013 | access-date=14 June 2015 | author=Walsh, Kevin}}</ref>

Horse Brook Island is a traffic island at the intersection of 90th Street, Justice Avenue, and 56th Avenue.<ref name="libra triangle"/> The traffic island is reminiscent of the former [[Horse Brook (Queens)|Horse Brook]], a [[creek (stream)|creek]] that flowed to the [[Flushing River]] from the present-day intersection of Kneeland Avenue and Codwise Place.<ref name="fny"/><ref>{{cite Hidden Waters NYC|pages=122-131}}</ref> The space was renovated from 1986 to 1994.<ref name="libra triangle">{{cite web | url=http://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/libra-triangle/highlights/12231 | title=Libra Triangle Horsebrook Island | publisher=[[New York City Department of Parks and Recreation]] | access-date=June 8, 2015}}</ref>

Justice Avenue, an Elmhurst road that has existed since [[Colonial history of the United States|the American colonial period]], follows an unusual curved path through Elmhurst due to a now-defunct railroad line immediately to the south.<ref name="fny"/> Its name relates to the former Newtown Town Hall that stood at the intersection of Justice Avenue and Broadway.<ref>{{cite web | last=Kadinsky| first=Sergey| title=Newtown Town Hall | website=[[Forgotten NY|Forgotten-NY]] | date=2022-02-20| url=https://forgotten-ny.com/2022/02/newtown-hall/ | access-date=2025-07-24}}</ref>

[[Queens Boulevard]], a wide at-grade highway that stretches from [[Long Island City]] to [[Jamaica, Queens|Jamaica]], was formerly composed of two small dirt roads: Old Jamaica Road and Hoffman Boulevard. In the 1910s, it was paved and widened to 12 lanes. It is sometimes called the "Boulevard of Death" because of the high fatality rate on Queens Boulevard.<ref name="fny"/>

The majority of Whitney Avenue, which stretches from 83rd Street in the west to [[Roosevelt Avenue]] and 93rd Street to the northeast, is on a tilted street grid, developed in the early 20th century. The street grid consists of Broadway; Aske, Benham, Case, Denman, Elbertson, Forley, Gleane, Hampton, Ithaca, Judge, Ketcham, Layton, Macnish Streets; Ketcham Place; and Baxter, Pettit, Britton, Vietor, Elmhurst, Whitney, and Lamont Avenues. Whitney Avenue also has the most religious institutions of any street in Elmhurst.<ref name="whitney">{{cite web | url=http://forgotten-ny.com/2014/03/whitney-avenue-holiness-elmhurst/ | title=WHITNEY AVENUE HOLINESS, Elmhurst | publisher=Forgotten NY | date=March 2014 | access-date=14 June 2015 | author=Walsh, Kevin}}</ref>

[[Woodhaven Boulevard]] was known as Trotting Course Lane because it was named when horses were the main mode of transport. Although it extends to Cross Bay Boulevard in [[the Rockaways]], two small parts of the original lane still exist in [[Forest Hills, Queens|Forest Hills]].<ref>*{{cite web | url=http://forgotten-ny.com/1999/05/woodhaven-trotting-course/ | title=WOODHAVEN TROTTING COURSE | work=Forgotten NY | date=May 1999 | access-date=June 13, 2015 | author=Walsh, Kevin}}
*{{cite web | url=http://forgotten-ny.com/2013/11/trotting-course-lane-forest-hills/ | title=TROTTING COURSE LANE, Forest Hills | publisher=Forgotten NY | date=November 2013 | access-date=June 14, 2015 | author=Walsh, Kevin}}</ref>

==Parks==
[[File:QueensVietnamVeteransMemorialAM.jpg|thumb|[[Queens Vietnam Veterans Memorial]] in [[Elmhurst Park]]]]

[[Elmhurst Park]] is on 57th Avenue west of 80th Street. There is a children's playground with slides, swings, and exercise machines, as well as walking paths and a lawn atop a hill. The land for the park was formerly occupied by gas tanks. The park itself was opened in 2011.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/elmhurstpark/ |title=Elmhurst Park : NYC Parks |publisher=Nycgovparks.org |date=2011-05-24 |access-date=December 12, 2013}}</ref> It includes the [[Queens Vietnam Veterans Memorial]], which was finished in 2019.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.qchron.com/editions/queenswide/they-remain-ageless-in-our-minds-vet/article_3898f9f3-7a7d-531c-b425-5535f8b4adaf.html|title='They remain ageless in our minds': vet|last=Russell|first=David|date=December 26, 2019|website=Queens Chronicle|access-date=2019-12-29}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://queenseagle.com/all/2019/12/27/queens-first-vietnam-war-memorial-finally-opens-in-elmhurst|title=Queens' first Vietnam War Memorial finally opens in Elmhurst|last=Brand|first=David|date=December 27, 2019|website=Queens Daily Eagle|language=en-US|access-date=2019-12-29}}</ref>

Moore Homestead Park is located between Broadway and 45th Avenue. There is a children's playground with slides and swings and there are different sections where people can play basketball, handball, and chess. The park is named after a nearby [[homestead (buildings)|homestead]] owned by [[Clement Clarke Moore]], whose ancestor John Moore helped negotiate Newtown's land area with the Native American population there. The park, originally acquired by the [[Independent Subway System]] and then turned into a playground, was renovated in the 1990s, and again in the 2020s.<ref>{{cite web | title=Moore Homestead Playground Highlights : NYC Parks | website=New York City Department of Parks & Recreation | url=http://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/moore-homestead-playground/history | access-date=2015-09-22}}</ref>

Frank D. O'Connor Playground is located on Broadway between Woodside Avenue and 78th Street. There is also a children playground, basketball and handball area. Opened in 1937 and renovated in 1996, the park is named after former state senator [[Frank D. O'Connor]].<ref>{{cite web | title=Frank D. O'Connor Playground Highlights: NYC Parks | website=New York City Department of Parks & Recreation | url=http://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/frank-d-oconnor-playground/history | access-date=2015-09-22}}</ref>

Veterans Grove is located on 43rd Avenue by Judge and Ketcham Streets. It is a small park mainly for younger children. The park's plaque states that it was dedicated "to the memory of those soldiers from Elmhurst who lost their lives serving in [[World War I]]." The park land was acquired in 1928, and the park was originally called the Elmhurst Memorial Park. It was renovated in 1994–6.<ref>{{cite web | title=Veterans Grove Highlights | website=New York City Department of Parks & Recreation | url=http://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/veterans-grove/history | access-date=2015-09-22}}</ref>

[[Horse Brook (Queens)|Horsebrook Island]] is a small triangular green space at the junction of 56th Avenue, Justice Avenue and 90th Street that was named after a stream that once ran through the Newtown settlement. The creek was buried in the first three decades of the twentieth century.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://forgotten-ny.com/2008/03/our-mr-brook-sergey-kadinsky-follows-the-former-horse-brook/|title=HORSE BROOK, Queens - Forgotten New York|date=March 22, 2008|access-date=July 7, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/horsebrook-island-q152/highlights/12231|title=Horsebrook Island Highlights - Horsebrook Island : NYC Parks|access-date=July 7, 2016}}</ref>

[[Libra Triangle]] is a small triangular green space at the junction of Justice Avenue and Broadway.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/horsebrook-island-q152/history |title=Libra Triangle|publisher= [[New York City Department of Parks & Recreation]]|website=nycgovparks.org|access-date=2016-07-07}}</ref>

Newtown Playground is located on 92nd Street and 56th Avenue. There are two children's playgrounds, chess tables, swings, sprinklers, and a small lawn. The park is named after the original name of Elmhurst given by the English. It is one block away from [[Queens Center|Queens Center Mall]] and Newtown High School's athletic field.

== Education ==
{{Further|New York City Department of Education}}
Elmhurst and Corona generally have a lower ratio of college educated residents than the rest of the city {{as of|2018|lc=y}}. While 28% of residents age 25 and older have a college education or higher, 30% have less than a high school education and 42% are high school graduates or have some college education. By contrast, 39% of Queens residents and 43% of city residents have a college education or higher.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}} The percentage of Elmhurst and Corona students excelling in math rose from 36% in 2000 to 66% in 2011, and reading achievement rose from 42% to 49% during the same time period.<ref name=":17">{{Cite web|url=http://furmancenter.org/files/sotc/QN_04_11.pdf|title=Elmhurst/Corona – QN 04|date=2011|publisher=[[Furman Center for Real Estate and Urban Policy]]|access-date=October 5, 2016}}</ref>

Elmhurst and Corona's rate of elementary school student absenteeism is less than the rest of New York City. In Elmhurst and Corona, 11% of elementary school students missed twenty or more days per [[school year]], lower than the citywide average of 20%.<ref name=":21" />{{Rp|24 (PDF p. 55)}}<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}} Additionally, 81% of high school students in Elmhurst and Corona graduate on time, more than the citywide average of 75%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}}

==Transportation==
[[New York City Subway]] stations include [[Jackson Heights–Roosevelt Avenue (IND Queens Boulevard Line)|Jackson Heights–Roosevelt Avenue]], [[Woodhaven Boulevard (IND Queens Boulevard Line)|Woodhaven Boulevard]], [[Grand Avenue–Newtown (IND Queens Boulevard Line)|Grand Avenue–Newtown]], and [[Elmhurst Avenue (IND Queens Boulevard Line)|Elmhurst Avenue]], all served by the {{NYCS trains|Queens local}} of the [[IND Queens Boulevard Line]]. In addition, the [[IRT Flushing Line]], served by the {{NYCS trains|Flushing}}, runs along Roosevelt Avenue, the north border of Elmhurst, with stations at [[74th Street–Broadway (IRT Flushing Line)|74th Street–Broadway]], [[82nd Street–Jackson Heights (IRT Flushing Line)|82nd Street–Jackson Heights]], and [[90th Street–Elmhurst Avenue (IRT Flushing Line)|90th Street–Elmhurst Avenue]].<ref>{{NYCS const|map|mdy=yes}}</ref>

Elmhurst is bounded by the [[Long Island Expressway]] to the south and by the [[Brooklyn-Queens Expressway]] to the west. [[Queens Boulevard]], [[Woodhaven Boulevard]], Junction Boulevard, [[Roosevelt Avenue]], and [[Broadway (Queens)|Broadway]] are major roads in the community. Elmhurst is connected to Manhattan and Jamaica by Queens Boulevard, and is connected to [[John F. Kennedy International Airport]] by Woodhaven Boulevard and to [[LaGuardia Airport]] by Junction Boulevard.<ref>{{google maps|url=https://www.google.com/maps/place/Elmhurst,+Queens,+NY/@40.7382526,-73.8812746,15z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m2!3m1!1s0x89c25e53a0cfe215:0xf2b5b46ba0fdbb70|title=Elmhurst, NY|access-date=June 8, 2015}}</ref>

==In popular culture==
McDowell's, the fictional restaurant depicted in the 1988 film ''[[Coming to America]]'', is located in Elmhurst. For the week-long shot, the filmmakers cosmetically altered an existing [[Wendy's]] restaurant, which was closed in May 2013 and was razed by December 2013 to make way for condominiums.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://gothamist.com/2013/06/16/beloved_coming_to_america_restauran.php | title=Beloved Coming To America Restaurant McDowell's Will Soon Be Demolished | work=[[Gothamist]] | date=June 16, 2013 | access-date=June 14, 2015 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150509221424/http://gothamist.com/2013/06/16/beloved_coming_to_america_restauran.php | archive-date=May 9, 2015 | df=mdy-all }}</ref> Images of surrounding streets were also used in the movie.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://blogs.wsj.com/metropolis/2013/06/14/queens-boulevard-loses-a-movie-icon-disguised-as-a-fast-food-joint/?mod=WSJBlog | title=Queens Boulevard Loses a Movie Icon, Disguised as a Fast Food Joint | work=Wall Street Journal Blog | date=June 14, 2013 | access-date=June 14, 2015 | author=Hirshon, Nicholas}}</ref>

The CBS show [[Blue Bloods (TV series)|''Blue Bloods'']] filmed for its third season on the residential streets of Elmhurst in 2012.

Part of the ''[[Revenge of the Green Dragons]]'' was filmed in Elmhurst with cameos from locals.<ref>Chang, Justin. [https://variety.com/2014/film/festivals/film-review-revenge-of-the-green-dragons-1201340823/ "Film Review: ''Revenge of the Green Dragons''"], ''[[Variety (magazine)]]'', October 28, 2014. Accessed July 20, 2016. "As laid out in Fredric Dannen's detailed 1992 New Yorker account (the authoritative basis for Loo and Michael Di Jiacomo's patched-together script), the Green Dragons were a ruthless street gang in Elmhurst, Queens, consisting primarily of first-generation Chinese youths whose awareness of their third-class citizenship bred a particularly menacing form of social rebellion."</ref>
